2Wild fleet report · 2026-09-01

NVFP4 vs EXL3 on DGX Spark

The same 320B MoE, GLM-5.3-Flash, in two 4-bit quantizations, on two independent 2-node DGX Spark pairs, benched at the same time, isolated from every other consumer. Full c1–c6 sweep: throughput, per-stream decode, time to first token, wall-to-wall latency, prefill, context, KV pool.

4× DGX Spark GB10 · 128 GB UMACX7 RoCE rail 0 · TP=2 per lanevLLM · DFlash2 k=7 · fp8 KVnon-stream · temp 0 · thinking off@tonyd2wild
1.7×
faster single-stream decode (61.2 vs 38.3 tok/s)
5.7×
faster prefill (3,217 vs 565 tok/s) · TTFT 0.50 s vs 2.87 s
4.7×
the KV pool (1,396,551 vs 295,230 tokens) · 1M vs 256K context

Result. EXL3 / TR3 4bpw won every throughput and latency line we measured, was an order of magnitude more stable run-to-run (±0.5% vs ±16%), served four times the context with 4.7× the KV pool on identical hardware, and gave an identical answer on the quality probe. NVFP4's published warm figure is 46.9 tok/s single-stream; EXL3 is still +30% against that.

Hardware and topology

Four NVIDIA DGX Spark boxes (GB10 superchip, sm_121a, 128 GB unified memory, ~121 GB usable), ring-connected over a ConnectX-7 RoCE v2 fabric on 192.168.192.0/24, rail 0 (enp1s0f0np0 / rocep1s0f0, GID index 3). Reddie (.2) heads the NVFP4 lane with Spark4 (.4) as its worker; Bluey (.1) heads the EXL3 lane with Asusi (.3). Both lanes are tensor-parallel 2 across two nodes with vLLM's multiprocess executor and NCCL over RoCE. They share nothing but the switch. The bench client was a Mac mini on the same tailnet.

The two lanes

NVFP4, the reference lane

The published 2-Spark recipe, tonyd2wild/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4-DFlash2-2x-DGX-Spark, run verbatim. Weights RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4; image ghcr.io/tonyd2wild/vllm-glm53-flash:sm121-v11-dflash2 with the sm121 sparse-attention patch; --max-model-len 262144 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --kv-cache-memory 3 GiB --max-num-seqs 6 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --block-size 2304 --moe-backend marlin --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --enforce-eager; DFlash2 drafter incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2, k=7; vm.swappiness=0; worker first, head 25 s later. The repo's own figures: ~15 min boot, 46.9 tok/s single-stream (code, warm), 47.7 tok/s c6 aggregate.

EXL3, the challenger

The Reederey87 GB10 kit, with MiaAI-Lab's sibling as cross-reference, built for our fabric. Weights brandonmusic/GLM-5.3-Flash-tr3-4bpw, EXL3 / TR3 trellis at 4 bits per weight, 120 shards, ~164 GiB, ~91 GiB resident per node; image built on the head from the kit's Dockerfile (exllamav3 compiled for 12.1a); --quantization exl3 --max-model-len 1000000 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 15414698763 --max-num-seqs 4 --max-num-batched-tokens 3584 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --no-async-scheduling; the same DFlash2 drafter at k=7 (~40% acceptance). About 12 minutes to serve. Every fix we needed is in our fork, tonyd2wild/glm53-flash-exl3-2x-dgx-spark.

Both lanes: fp8 KV cache, thinking disabled, the multimodal chat template, native image_url input (a 64×64 red square came back "Red" on both).

Method

Isolation. Before measuring, every other consumer was moved off both lanes: the spark-flash relay our external agents use was parked on the 3090's Qwen 27B, the latency dashboard (which sends real probe completions, not just metric scrapes) was paused, and the three Hermes supervisors whose default model is glm-5.3-flash were moved to the 27B. After each run we pulled each head's access log: every chat POST in the window came from the bench client, and the counts matched the requests issued. The supervisors run on the same Mac as the bench client, so the IP alone proves nothing; the request counts do.

Simultaneity. The two lanes were benched in parallel. They share no GPUs, no memory, and no NCCL group, so parallel runs do not contend; it halves wall time and removes time-of-day drift.

Warm-up. Both engines JIT-compile kernels lazily per request shape. Every lane got 2× c1 + 1× c6 warm-up requests before measurement. The first-ever completion on a fresh EXL3 boot was ~30 tok/s and its first long prefill 136 tok/s; both settle after one warm request. NVFP4's first request after boot took 5.2 s, the third 3.3 s. Never bench a cold lane.

Metrics. Throughput is median tokens per second, non-streaming. c1: 5 sequential ~300-token generations. c2–c6: 3 rounds of c concurrent generations; aggregate = Σ tokens / round wall; per-stream = each request's tokens / its own wall; wall-to-wall = each request's end-to-end latency (median and p90). TTFT at level c: c concurrent ~1.5K-token prompts with an 8-token answer, median wall. Prefill = prompt tokens / that wall at c1. All requests temperature 0, stream false, thinking off, identical prompts to both lanes. Tools: tools/bench_sweep.py, tools/bench_detailed.py, tools/quality_probe.py in the repo.

Reading the curve. EXL3 scales almost linearly to 149.6 tok/s at c4, then flattens to 114–124 at c5–c6 while its p90 wall-to-wall jumps from 8.9 s to 14–15 s. That is the kit's --max-num-seqs 4: the fifth and sixth requests wait behind a full batch. It is a configuration cap, not the quantization, and raising it is the obvious next experiment. NVFP4 (--max-num-seqs 6) admits all six but pays per stream: 38.3 → 21.0 tok/s, TTFT 2.9 → 9.8 s. Its c4 dip (66 < c3's 95) reproduced across two independent sweeps, so it is real.

Reproducibility. NVFP4 was swept twice, the second time after every agent had been moved off the lane (0 requests in the 3 minutes before). Run 1 and run 2 agreed within 3% at every level. EXL3's five c1 runs spanned 60.9–61.5.

Quality

Same prompt to both, thinking off, temperature 0: write top_k_frequent(nums, k) in O(n log k) with an explanation and an edge case, and solve the bat-and-ball trap ($1.10 total, the bat $1.00 more than the ball). Both lanes answered both parts correctly, with the algebra written out and a check line, and ANSWER: $0.05. The diff between the answers is cosmetic. Published KLD figures put EXL3/TR3 4bpw near 0.025 (tying FP8) and NVFP4 near 0.060, so a quality gap is expected to exist; on a probe of this difficulty it did not surface. Harder probes are the open items.

Discussion

Where the speed comes from. The largest gap is prefill, 5.7×. EXL3's fused trellis MoE kernels prefill a 1.5K prompt in half a second; the NVFP4 marlin path took 2.9 s. For agents that is the number users feel: time to first token. Decode is 1.6–1.7× faster and holds at concurrency.

On NVFP4's numbers. They sit below the repo's published 46.9 c1 / 47.7 c6-aggregate on the code prompt; on our count-to-300 prompt they reproduced at 38.3 across two sweeps. Its worker loaded weights over NFS from the head because Spark4 had no local copy of the base, which lengthened boot to ~40 minutes but should not affect decode. None of this closes a 1.6× gap; even at 46.9, EXL3 is +30% on c1.

Context and KV. EXL3 serves 1,048,576 tokens of context with a 1,396,551-token KV pool on the same two boxes on which the NVFP4 recipe serves 262,144 with a 295,230-token pool. We learned the hard way that NVFP4 at TP2 cannot be launched at 1M: an adapted launcher with --max-model-len 1048576 and a pinned 8 GiB KV produced three worker reboots on NVRM: NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY at cudagraph capture and a 24-minute stall at the profiling pass, until the published 256K recipe was run verbatim.

Memory. Each lane holds ~91 GiB of weights per 121 GiB node. Every failure we hit was a transient spike on top of that baseline: cudagraph capture, the profiling forward pass, page cache inflated by a 164 GiB rsync. Drop caches on every node before every launch; free -g under-reports on GB10.

What broke, and the fixes

  • EXL3 kit: count_shards() used find -type f, which misses the symlinks a standard HF cache uses → "0 / 120 shards". Fix: find -L.
  • EXL3 kit: the worker needs the full ~164 GiB on disk; vLLM TP reads slices of every shard.
  • EXL3 kit: a root-owned ~/.cache/vllm-glm53-flash makes mkdir tilelang fail and the launch exit with no containers. chown it on both nodes.
  • EXL3 kit: it binds --host 127.0.0.1; unreachable off-box. Set 0.0.0.0.
  • Both: after a large file move, the memory gate stalls on page cache — drop caches.
  • NVFP4: run the published recipe verbatim before adapting anything. vm.swappiness=0 does not survive reboot. The head's "No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds" is benign while a worker is compiling and only fatal when the worker is actually dead. Poll /health, not /v1/models.

Reproduce

# NVFP4, both nodes: pull the image, weights at /var/tmp/glm-5.3-flash-nvfp4 (or NFS from the head),
# drafter at /var/tmp/models/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2, patch at ~/patches/sparse_attn_indexer_kpool.py
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=0; sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
./launch-glm53-vllm-tp2-dflash2.sh 1      # worker
sleep 25; ./launch-glm53-vllm-tp2-dflash2.sh 0   # head
until curl -sf http://<head>:8000/health; do sleep 20; done

# EXL3, on the head: clone tonyd2wild/glm53-flash-exl3-2x-dgx-spark
docker build -t glm53-flash-sm121:local .
cp .env.example .env    # node IPs, WORKER_SSH, RoCE NIC + GID (verify /sys/class/infiniband/<hca>/ports/1/gids/3)
sudo chown -R $USER ~/.cache/vllm-glm53-flash   # both nodes
sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches # both nodes
set -a; . ./.env; set +a; ./local/prod-start.sh

# bench, per lane, with everything else moved off it first
python3 tools/bench_sweep.py http://<head>:8000 <served-model> "<label>" --rounds 3 --max-c 6

Caveats and what's next

  • One quality probe is not a quality study. Open: multi-file refactor correctness, tool-call argument validity, long-context recall past 200K.
  • Raise EXL3's --max-num-seqs and re-sweep c5–c8; re-bench NVFP4 with the repo's code prompt after a long soak.
  • Neither lane here is the abliterated variant; both are the base model.
  • Two specific quants on one specific cluster. The literature says EXL3 should win on quality-per-bit; what we measured is that on this hardware it also wins on speed, decisively.
